Concept Explanation

Core technical principle: The docs show that generic data tests in dbt are simply SQL “test” blocks that live in your project and accept standard arguments. As the documentation states, “Generic tests are defined in SQL files” and you should “create a `test` block called ``.” These blocks use the standard arguments (`model`, `column_name`) — the docs say “All generic tests should accept one or both of the standard arguments: model … column_name.” The behavioral contract is also explicit: the test body is a SELECT that reports failing rows — “If this `select` statement returns zero records, then every record in the supplied `model` argument is even!” (the is_even example demonstrates this pattern).

In short: a generic test is a reusable SQL rule (a test block) that dbt runs against a templated relation (`{{ model }}`) and column (`{{ column_name }}`) to surface validation rows when the test fails.

Implementation considerations: follow the documented shape and placement. The docs show two valid locations: “`tests/generic/`: … a special subfolder named `generic` within your test paths” or `macros/` when you need macro logic.

If you need extra parameters, the docs instruct you to “include those arguments in the test signature” (see the relationships example that adds `field` and `to`). If you want default behavior like severity, the docs explain “It is possible to include a `config()` block in a generic test definition.

Values set there will set defaults for all specific instances of that generic test…” and illustrate `{{ config(severity = 'warn') }}`. The docs also recommend documenting test macros by adding a description under `macros:` in schema.yml: “You can add a description to the Jinja macro that provides the core logic for a data test by including the `description` key under the `macros:` section.” Why common alternatives are problematic (documentation-backed): the docs present compact, set-based examples (e.g., the is_even test builds a validation CTE and then filters to validation_errors) — the intended pattern is a single SELECT that returns offending rows.

Because the contract is a SELECT over `{{ model }}`, the docs’ examples favor set-based expressions (CTEs, filters, groupings) rather than pairwise comparisons. The docs also call out that defaults set with config() change behavior: their example shows `{{ config(severity = 'warn') }}` and warns implicitly that “Any time the `warn_if_odd` test is used, it will *always* have warning-level severity, unless the specific test overrides that value.” That means forcing a warning-level default on your override changes the semantics of every test instance unless explicitly overridden.

Finally, the examples use aliases (the is_even example aliases the selected column as `even_field`) — following that pattern makes the test logic clearer and easier to maintain than recomputing an expression multiple times.

Best practices and practical impact: the docs make it explicit how to take ownership of built-ins: “To change the way a built-in generic test works … you simply add a test block named `` to your own project. dbt will favor your version over the global implementation!” That is the sanctioned way to implement your domain rules (for example, case-insensitive email uniqueness and ignoring soft-deleted rows).

The docs also instruct you to document your custom test (add `description` and argument docs under `macros:`) so maintainers understand intent and arguments. Practically, because a generic test is just SQL run against the relation you pass in, the performance and correctness consequences are exactly the same as any query you would write against that table: choose set-based constructs and clear aliases (as the examples do) and be deliberate about any `config()` defaults you embed, because those defaults change how every instance of the test behaves unless overridden.
